situation:
You and your teammate serve as the marketing director and the member services manager at BRIGHTLINK TELEHEALTH COOPERATIVE, a worker-owned telehealth practice providing virtual primary care and behavioral health visits. The cooperative's executive director (judge) has asked to meet with you today. Roughly 140 clinicians and staff hold ownership shares in the cooperative and vote on decisions that affect their own employment, a structure the cooperative treats as central to both its culture and its pitch to prospective patients.

Nine years ago, three home-health nurses founded the cooperative after growing frustrated with staffing agencies that treated clinicians as replaceable. Word of mouth built the patient base for several years, until a referral partnership with ALDERGROVE HEALTH PARTNERS, a regional hospital system, began sending a steady stream of new patients two years ago. That single relationship now accounts for close to forty percent of new patient visits, and the cooperative's marketing leans heavily on Aldergrove's name in its outreach materials to prospective patients.

A staff outreach coordinator filed a harassment complaint against a founding worker-owner clinician, alleging repeated unwelcome comments during a training session. The cooperative opened an internal investigation, and its ethics panel is not scheduled to convene for three weeks. Aldergrove's referral contract contains a conduct clause requiring the cooperative to suspend, without pay, any clinician named in an open harassment investigation, or Aldergrove may end the referral agreement on thirty days' notice. The cooperative's own operating agreement, ratified by every worker-owner, guarantees a hearing before the ethics panel before any suspension without pay takes effect.

Suspending the clinician now would satisfy Aldergrove's contract and protect the referral relationship the cooperative's growth depends on, but it would take away a worker-owner's income and voice in cooperative decisions before the peers who elected the ethics panel have heard the case, a step no worker-owner has faced in the cooperative's nine-year history. Waiting for the panel would honor the operating agreement every worker-owner signed, but it would leave the cooperative's referral contract exposed at a time when Aldergrove has other telehealth practices seeking the same partnership.

The executive director (judge) has asked your team to analyze the cooperative's obligations to Aldergrove and to its own worker-owners, and to recommend how the cooperative should proceed before the ethics panel meets. The recommendation should address what the cooperative communicates to Aldergrove about the investigation, what it communicates to its worker-owners about how the decision was reached, and how the complaint continues to be investigated fairly while that recommendation is carried out.

You will have 30 minutes to review this situation carefully and plan your presentation together with your teammate. The executive director (judge) will then greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and expect a clear, well-supported recommendation. At the conclusion of your presentation, the executive director (judge) will thank you both for your work.
judgeCharacterization: You are the executive director (judge) of BRIGHTLINK TELEHEALTH COOPERATIVE. Business background is the same as the situation above. You want the participants to analyze the cooperative's obligations to Aldergrove and to its own worker-owners, and to recommend how the cooperative should proceed before the ethics panel meets.
judgeQuestions: What would you say to the outreach coordinator who filed the complaint if the clinician is not suspended right away?
